# Generate and edit images

Use `connector__matrix__generate_image` for new images and edits that change image content.
[model-spec.md](references/model-spec.md) covers the model's limits, strengths, and prompt craft.
Preserve the user's visual intent, source images, and requested specifications through delivery.

Use the image model for every change to image content, including corrections requested after
delivery. Do not use compositing tools, other image editors, or Python or other code to repair,
retouch, or combine images unless the user explicitly requests that specific tool or method.
A request to fix or modify an image must go through the image model. Deliver the returned image
directly without adding an inspection, verification script, or repair pass on your own.
Follow the [completion and delivery rules](#execute-and-deliver) after each edit.

This skill applies when the deliverable is an image. When the user wants text instead, such as a
translation, a description, or details read from an image, read the image and answer in text
yourself.

Use the image model whenever the user wants an image designed, created, or changed, including work
that demands precision. It handles typography, placement, layout, counts, and preservation, so put
these requirements in the prompt. Send the user's original images, not crops, mirrored copies, or
merged boards.

## What the model does in one call

Each item below is a kind of job the model finishes in a single request. The examples show typical
uses, not a complete list.

- **Many pictures in one image.** Grids, storyboards, comic pages, icon, sticker, and sprite sheets,
  comparisons, step-by-step guides, and tables or layouts with small illustrations. The model draws
  the whole sheet in one pass, with its frames, captions, numbers, arrows, and connecting lines, and
  keeps recurring characters, products, style, lighting, and background consistent from panel to
  panel. For example, one screen that walks through a process step by step or a motion frame by
  frame, or a board that shows a brand's logo, key visuals, and variations together.
- **Layout and lettering.** Posters, covers, infographics, charts, plans, schedules, resumes, and
  labels, with copy in Chinese, English, and other languages, placed in the hierarchy the prompt
  gives. For example, a page whose headline, body copy, and images follow a clear hierarchy, or a
  diagram whose parts carry labels and numbered callouts.
- **Reasoning.** It reads the documents, exam sheets, papers, plans, maps, photos, and annotated
  sketches the user supplies, works out what the brief asks, and draws the result. Pass the problem
  through instead of solving it yourself. For example, an answer or result worked out from the
  material and drawn in place, or a view or finished form inferred from a drawing, map, or flat
  layout.
- **Transforming a whole image.** It changes the style, medium, lighting, season, or level of finish
  while keeping the composition, the structure, and how the objects relate. For example, a photo,
  sketch, or model screenshot re-rendered in another style or finish, or the same scene moved to
  another season, time of day, or light.
- **Clean-up into a final version.** It turns photographed, cluttered, or damaged material into a
  clean version with the same content. For example, photographed pages as flat, ordered scans, or a
  blurred, faded, or damaged photo restored to a clear one.
- **Precise edits** to light, viewpoint, objects, materials, lettering, and layout. Send these edits
  to the model with the user's preservation requirements, including pixel-level consistency when
  requested. For example, one object, word, or material changed while the rest stays, or the canvas
  extended to a new ratio around unchanged content.
- **Compositing.** It places people, products, logos, and other subjects from the references into a
  new picture, keeping their identity, shape, color, and labels, and matching light and perspective.
  It also cuts, nests, and rearranges shapes taken from the references. For example, a product,
  person, or logo placed into a new scene or onto a surface it follows, or parts of several pictures
  cut and recombined into a new arrangement.
- **Graphic design.** Logos, wordmarks, icon sets, packaging, and UI boards, in flat, vector-style,
  or any other look, consistent across a set. For example, a brand mark or wordmark, or a family of
  icons, packaging, or screens that share one visual language.
- **Styles** such as pixel art, vector-style logos and icons, technical illustrations, and
  texture maps.

An image made of many smaller pictures is still one image for the model, and one request returns
it finished. Edit an existing one as a whole, build one from several references in a single
request, or create one from text alone, such as a five-day weather forecast. Do not split the work
into parts and assemble them. In the prompt, name the layout and, for a grid, each panel's aspect
ratio, such as a 3×3 grid of 16:9 panels. Keep recurring characters and the style consistent with
the references that supply them, or describe them once when there are none. Then describe each
picture in reading order, or tell a short story for the model to lay out.

## Keep the requested scope

Match your actions to the user's intended outcome. Do not expand a request for information into
creating or modifying artifacts.

Keep the total number of images within the user's request, including any delegated image tasks.
Do not generate preliminary images or extra alternatives unless the user requests them.

## Choose the workflow

- **Text to image.** Start with the intended use, subject, and framing. If the brief requires an
  exact likeness of the user's subject, ask for a reference image when it is missing.
- **Edit.** Identify the base image and the requested change. Use the version the user names, even
  when there is a newer one. Keep its framing by default. Read [edit.md](references/edit.md).
- **Generate from references.** A reference can supply any aspect of the new image, such as the
  people, products, or objects in it, its scene, layout, pose, camera, style, palette, lettering,
  light, or material, and each picture can supply a different aspect. Tell the model what to take
  from each picture, in the user's terms. Read
  [reference-generation.md](references/reference-generation.md).
- **Prompt only.** Apply the relevant guidance and return one prompt unless the user requests
  variants. For this Connector, put exclusions in the same `prompt` string. If suggesting settings,
  give one compatible set from [model-spec.md](references/model-spec.md).
  Deliver the prompt directly. Stop before Connector discovery, upload, or generation, including
  test renders or a separate verification task to evaluate the prompt.

Any request with a reference image, one or many, takes the same edit path. These workflows differ in
how the prompt assigns each image's role: adding elements to a base image is an edit, and a new
composition built from several images is reference generation.

Ask a focused question when the base image, reference role, or requested edit is ambiguous enough to
change the deliverable. A poster request with an attached photo could mean adding copy to that photo
or designing a new poster that uses its subject. Read [text.md](references/text.md) when the image
contains important lettering or the brief calls for adding, changing, translating, or excluding text.

For a standalone cutout or enhancement, use the dedicated image tool. For a combined request, use
the generation tool for the content change, then apply the dedicated operation to its result. Check
that both tools are available before submitting. If a dedicated operation is unavailable, explain
the limitation and ask before substituting a generative edit.

For a transparent image, follow the background-removal workflow in
[delivery.md](references/delivery.md). Deliver both the
source image with its background and the transparent result.

## Prepare the prompt

Read [model-spec.md](references/model-spec.md) before writing. When the user says what to change or
create, pass that instruction to the model with the images, in the user's terms, without studying
the images first: the model sees them better than you do. Use the brief and conversation to resolve
each image's role, the target, and the requested change. Inspect only the relevant images when this
context leaves an ambiguity that would change the result; ask if it remains unresolved. Missing
Picture/Image numbering alone does not require inspection. Refer to each image as Picture 1,
Picture 2, and so on, in `reference_images` order. Write the prompt in the user's
language by default and quote required visible text as supplied. Use the intended purpose to choose
output settings.

Read the links the user provides, and look up current or specialized facts the image needs but the
user did not give, such as dates, prices, weather, or specifications, and write them into the
prompt. Do not look up answers the model can work out from the supplied material, or collect
reference photos on your own. When you set a ratio, describe the same canvas in the prompt, such
as a vertical 9:16 composition.

Preserve decisions in detailed briefs and add only details needed to realize shorter ones, drawing
on the brief and its purpose rather than a study of the images. Add visible text only when
requested. Use the user's wording verbatim when requested. For a revision, start from the selected
image, carry forward the relevant preservation requirements, and focus the new prompt on the
remaining change.

## Check and submit the request

Load `mcode-tools-master` for CLI mechanics. Use the order in this skill for the image workflow.
Use [model-spec.md](references/model-spec.md) for all parameters and defaults, and follow
[preflight.md](references/preflight.md) to check the request against the live tool schema.
Preserve the user's explicit choices and resolve invalid or incompatible parameters before submission.

Submit the request as soon as it passes these checks. Do not ask the user to confirm the image
count, size, or cost. Ask a question only when an essential input is missing or the request is
ambiguous enough to change the deliverable. Retry a failed item once only after correcting an
actionable cause, then report anything that still fails. Do not automatically retry quota, balance,
or payment rejections while the relevant conditions remain unchanged, or change generation settings
or methods to bypass them. Explain the tool's returned reason and next steps. Verify the outcome of
a timed-out or interrupted call before submitting again.

## Execute and deliver

Follow [delivery.md](references/delivery.md) to upload inputs and submit the batch. Preserve the
full generation receipt, deliver successful images directly in the runtime's format, and report
failed items.

After image generation or editing succeeds, proceed directly to delivery of every
successful image, including all intermediate images.

Do not initiate any verification or validation of the generated results: do not
inspect the images, run checking scripts, or call other tools to check the output.
For image generation and editing, a successful tool result with returned asset
references is sufficient evidence to proceed to delivery. Do not add an
acceptance checklist, image inspection, verification script, or render-and-inspect
round before delivery unless the user explicitly requested that check for these
images in the current task.

Further tool use is limited to fetching, downloading, or delivering the returned
assets, and completing other operations explicitly requested by the user.
Review or verification is allowed only when specifically requested for the generated
results in the current task. General quality requirements or verification preferences
do not constitute such a request.

If the user requests background removal or a transparent background, call the dedicated
background-removal tool and deliver both the source image and the transparent result. Otherwise,
deliver the generated images directly without adding checks or post-processing on your own.
If further processing produces a different image, deliver both the original generated image and
the processed result. Label intermediate and final results clearly. A later failure must not hide
an earlier success.
Delivery completes the generation step; an additional visual acceptance stage is not part of it.

Requirements such as correct spelling, clean layout, exact placement, or preservation belong in the
generation prompt. They do not authorize a review, self-directed correction, or extra candidates.
Do not turn your own design choices into additional acceptance criteria. Use the successful receipt
to identify and deliver the returned asset directly.

Do not inspect, zoom in, crop, run OCR, or compare generated images before delivery unless the user
explicitly asks for a review. Do not denoise, recolor, composite, add text, regenerate, or export
extra variants unless the user asks for that change. Requested changes must use the image model;
do not implement them with code or another editor unless the user explicitly requests that method.
Keep pixel-level preservation requirements in the generation prompt; they do not authorize a custom
repair script or a different editing pipeline. Do not delete successful assets as part of choosing
a preferred result.

When the user asks for a review, compare once and report what you see; review alone does not
authorize another generation. When the user asks for a correction, use the image model to make the
requested change and deliver the returned image without another review-and-fix cycle. Keep the final
reply brief: report the images generated and any failed items. Do not claim that visual quality or
requirement compliance was verified unless that review was actually performed.

State assumptions that affect the result. If the Connector is unavailable, explain the limitation
and provide the prepared prompt when it can help the user continue.

===== references/model-spec.md =====
# Image model

The model generates images from text and edits images with references. One model serves
both, and any request with a reference image takes the edit path.

## Parameters and defaults

Generation settings follow the [text-to-image API](https://platform-pre.xaminim.com/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-generations)
and [image-editing API](https://platform-pre.xaminim.com/docs/api-reference/image-generation-h3-edits).
For `connector__matrix__generate_image`, wrap independent requests in `requests`; the generation
fields belong to each item. The runtime supplies model selection and transport.

| Field | Meaning and accepted values |
| --- | --- |
| `requests` | List of independent requests. Use separate items for different prompts. |
| `prompt` | Required, non-empty text; up to 32,000 Unicode characters after trimming surrounding whitespace. Include exclusions in this same string. |
| `reference_images` | Optional ordered list of 1–16 images. Each entry has a `url` from an upload or asset URL in the current environment, and an optional `mime_type` matching the file. Omit for text to image. |
| Reference files | JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC, or HEIF; at most 64 MiB each; each side 128–8192 pixels; long side at most four times the short side. |
| `aspect_ratio` | Optional; defaults to `auto`, chosen from the content and references. Also accepts `X:Y`, with X and Y integers from 1 to 300 and a ratio from 1:3 to 3:1, inclusive. |
| `area` | Optional; `1K`, `2K`, or `4K`, targeting about 1024², 2048², or 4096² pixels. Defaults to `4K`. Can be used independently of `aspect_ratio`. |
| `n` | Optional integer from 1 to 10 per request; defaults to 1. Each image is a separate file. A grid or sheet of panels is one image. |
| `output_format` | Optional; defaults to `jpeg`. Keep the default or explicitly set `jpeg`. Set `png` only when the user explicitly requests PNG. `jpg` and `jpeg` are equivalent, and the response reports `jpeg`. |
| `output_file` | Optional base filename. Choose an unused name; the service supplies the extension and appends `-1`, `-2`, etc. for multiple images. |

Choose the aspect ratio from the request and its purpose, such as `3:4` for a portrait cover, `9:16`
for a phone wallpaper, or `16:9` for a slide cover. For an edit that keeps the base image's framing,
use its ratio when supported. Otherwise, let the service choose. Keep the default area unless the
user asks for another tier, and request only the number of images the user wants.

Leave optional parameters at their defaults unless the request calls for a specific setting.
Use JPEG by default for high visual quality and fine detail with manageable file sizes. PNG files
are much larger. Generate and return PNG when the user explicitly requests it; otherwise use JPEG.

For example, a text-to-image request using the defaults:

```json
{
  "requests": [
    {
      "prompt": "3D render of a lamplit bookshop on a rainy evening, with a navy and amber palette.",
      "output_file": "rainy-bookshop"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Strengths

The model is especially strong at the following.

- 3D, CG, game screens, and game UI, including AAA-style game art.
- Turning comic and anime characters into photorealistic people in one step.
- Cinematic lighting.
- Hard physical details: hands working rope or string, complex mirror reflections, liquids in motion,
  and small figures in wide crowd scenes.
- Reading instructions drawn on an image, such as circles, arrows, and handwritten notes, and correcting
  typos in Chinese text.
- Faithful references: product structure, exploded views, and aligned multi-view drawings.
- Worked solutions: grading answers and setting out math and physics derivations.
- Clean explanatory layouts for education, finance, and medicine, and turning photographed documents
  into scans.
- One image with several consistent panels: grids, storyboards, sprite and icon sheets, comparisons,
  and step-by-step layouts.
- Reasoning from the brief and references: deductions, puzzles, exam answers written on an answer
  sheet, figures that match a paper, views from a map, and assembled forms from nets or exploded
  drawings.
- Multilingual lettering in posters, labels, and signs.
- Also: pixel and voxel art, collage, surreal photography, pen drawing, watercolor, felt stop-motion,
  traditional paper-cut, appetizing food, and old-photo restoration.

Use this list to send these tasks to the model, and to suggest directions when the user asks what
the model can do or leaves the direction open.

## Prompt craft

Describe the finished picture in concrete, visible terms. Keep what the brief already decides, and use
these details to fill what it leaves open. Editing, references, and lettering have their own guides.

- **Illustration, anime, or hand-drawn art.** Name the medium and finish instead of a genre word: line
  weight, shading method, brush or paper texture, palette, and a contemporary reference point. Ask for
  soft light, restrained saturation, and a richly detailed background.
- **Natural color.** Ask for natural saturation and a neutral white balance. Vivid looks need no request.
- **People.** Keep important faces in close or medium shots, and show distant figures from behind or in
  profile. Ask for a natural, even skin tone. Describe expressions by visible features, such as raised
  brows and a slight smile.
- **Posters and storyboards.** Give the visual hierarchy, focal point, and margins. For a grid, write
  every panel's shot size, subject, and action, and repeat one shared style block.
- **Facts and data.** Write the exact names, figures, and steps the user supplies or you looked up.
  When the brief asks the model to work out an answer from the supplied material, describe the task
  instead of the answer. For a chart, give every value and the axis range. For icons, routes, and
  schedules, pair each item with its label.
- **Positions.** Use image-relative terms such as upper left or foreground rather than compass
  directions.

## Prompts for each job

The model follows layouts, structures, and reasoning described in plain language, so the examples
below show how a request can read rather than a format to fill in. When the brief is already
detailed, or when you are unsure how to phrase it, send the user's original request as the prompt
and attach the pictures in the order it names them.

### Many pictures in one image

One request returns the whole sheet as a single image. The layout can be anything the brief
describes: a regular grid, a row of steps, a comic page with panels of different sizes, round,
triangular, or irregular frames, insets inside a larger picture, bands that blend into one another,
or a free collage. Describe recurring characters once or tie them to the pictures that supply them,
and set `aspect_ratio` when the layout fixes the overall shape. When the content is too much for
one legible sheet, split it into several sheets by section.

> Use Picture 1 as the first panel and continue the scene in eight more shots, as a 3×3 storyboard
> on one 16:9 canvas: panel 2, a medium close-up of her speaking; panel 3, his reverse shot as he
> listens; …

> A time-slice photo of a fishing harbor from one fixed camera on the opposite hillside, divided
> into five vertical bands that move from dawn to night and blend softly at their edges.

### Layout and lettering

The model sets out posters, cards, documents, charts, and diagrams with the hierarchy, positions,
and exact copy the brief gives, in any language.

> A 3:4 minimalist product poster on a seamless white backdrop: an oversized lemon low in the
> center, the words “酸得清醒” woven between its slices, and generous empty space above.

> A vintage 1890s United States patent sheet for a robotic arm, with numbered callouts, the title
> block, and inventor and witness signatures.

### Reasoning

The model works out what the brief asks from the supplied material and draws the result. Describe
the task, not the answer, and add only facts the model cannot see, such as the text of a linked
page.

> Split all the ingredients in Picture 1 evenly into two sandwiches with the same layers in the
> same order, cut each along one diagonal, and pack them into the two boxes shown.

> From the flat paper net in Picture 1, show the model fully folded, following its fold marks and
> tabs, as a studio product photo at a three-quarter view.

### Transforming a whole image

The model changes the style, medium, light, season, or finish of a whole picture while keeping its
composition and structure.

> Render the hand-drawn interior in Picture 1 as a photoreal view from the same camera, keeping its
> proportions, furniture, and design language, with real materials and daylight.

> Redraw this live-action still as realistic 2D animation, keeping each person's looks, clothes,
> and pose and the setting; change only the style.

### Clean-up into a final version

The model turns photographed, cluttered, or damaged material into a clean version with the same
content.

> Make the four pages photographed on a desk in Picture 1 into flat scans: each page upright and
> squared, shadows and glare removed, pages 1 to 4 in one row, and every word unchanged.

### Precise edits

The model changes what the brief names and keeps the rest of the picture as it was.

> Open both gates in Picture 1 inward by 90° on their original hinges, updating the perspective,
> overlaps, and shadows on the ground; keep everything else.

> Change the red paper ribbon in Picture 1 to satin of the same color, keeping its outline, its
> path through the rings, and what it covers; keep everything else.

### Compositing

The model places people, products, and logos from the references into a new picture and keeps
their identity, shape, color, and lettering.

> Put the cup from Picture 1 on a desk on a bright morning, beside a laptop and sticky notes, as
> the visual focus; keep its exact look, light it from the window, and add no ad text.

> Replace the platform outside the window in Picture 1 with a moonlit snowy forest, keeping the
> passengers, seats, and window frame in front of it and the raindrops on the glass.

### Graphic design

The model designs logos, wordmarks, icon sets, packaging, and interface boards in any look, and
keeps a set consistent.

> An original logo for a local bakery: clean, vector-like shapes, a strong silhouette, balanced
> negative space, and flat color that reads at small and large sizes, on a plain background.

For a transparent result, ask for a plain background that contrasts with the design; the
transparent workflow removes it.

# Generate with visual references

Upload the user's original images in the order the prompt uses, within the limits in
[model-spec.md](model-spec.md). Keep the original references separate.

Use the actual images the brief depends on. Give each input the purpose the user assigns it and
refer to it as Picture 1, Picture 2, and so on, in `reference_images` order.
Inputs carry no role field, so the prompt is the only place that says
which image is the base and what each one provides. Put the base canvas first when there is one.
Otherwise retain the user's order. Use the selected identity source for revisions so that
successive redraws do not compound drift.

Keep every reference the user supplied for this request unless they approve a narrower set. Keep
the originals intact. Follow the [prompt preparation rules](../SKILL.md#prepare-the-prompt) for
when to inspect a reference.

## Say what to take from each picture

A reference can supply any aspect of the new image: the people, characters, products, or objects
in it, its scene or setting, its layout and typography, a pose, a camera angle and framing, where
subjects stand, a style, a palette, light, a material, or a structure drawn in a sketch, plan, or
net. One picture can supply several aspects, and several pictures can supply the same kind, such
as three people for one scene. The core of the prompt is what to create and what to take from each
picture, written in the user's terms and sent with the original pictures. When a picture carries
more than the brief wants from it, such as its background or its copy, say what to leave out.

Describe the new composition and state which parts of each source contribute to it. Keep the roles
and labels consistent throughout the prompt. State how many times each subject appears, usually once,
and leave out watermarks and labels that are not part of the subject. When a source should
change form, name the target form, such as a clean printed form, instead of asking for an exact copy.

- **Person or character.** Refer to the subject by its picture, such as the character from
  Picture 1, and ask the model to keep their identity. Use the user's identification of the
  intended subject. Mention features or the rendering medium only when the user
  names them.
- **Product.** Preserve the exact shape, proportions, finish, logo, and readable label. If the angle
  stays and only the setting changes, treat the product photograph as the edit base. For a new view,
  tell the user that the model will infer the sides the photos do not show.
- **Visual style.** Point to the picture that supplies the style, such as the style of Picture 2,
  and name only the aspects the user picks, such as its palette. Take the subject, copy, and setting
  from the brief or their designated sources.
- **Pose or composition.** Specify what carries over, such as gesture, layout, or camera angle.
  Assign identity, clothing, and setting to their own sources when relevant.
- **Compositing.** Put the base scene first. Place each added element where the user wants it, and
  ask for matching scale, perspective, lighting, and contact shadows.
- **Virtual try-on.** Put the person first and the garment second. Preserve identity, body shape,
  pose, and framing. Transfer the garment's cut, fit, pattern, and logo from the reference. Specify
  plausible folds and lighting, and keep unrelated garments and accessories as they are.
- **Sketch to render.** Carry over layout, proportions, and perspective. Treat construction lines and
  handwritten directions as guides. Specify any lettering intended for the finished result.
- **Figurine or merchandise.** Identify the subject and describe the material, scale, finish, stand,
  packaging, and setting needed for the brief. Quote required logos or label text.
- **People from several pictures in one scene.** Name each person by their picture, say where each
  stands and what they do, and keep each identity. Take the place, light, and perspective from the
  scene's picture, and show each person once.
- **Layout and typography.** Name the picture that supplies the layout, type style, or palette, and
  the pictures or brief that supply the subject and the copy. Quote the new copy.
- **Scene or setting.** Name the picture that supplies the place. Say what of it stays, such as the
  room's shape, windows, and fixed furniture, and what changes, such as the time of day or the
  furnishing.
- **Light and color.** Name the picture whose light, time of day, or color grade the result should

- **Features from several pictures.** For a new design that mixes features, pair each feature with

    15→| `requests` | List of independent requests. Use separate items for different prompts. |
    16→| `prompt` | Required, non-empty text; up to 32,000 Unicode characters after trimming surrounding whitespace. Include exclusions in this same string. |
    17→| `reference_images` | Optional ordered list of 1–16 images. Each entry has a `url` from an upload or asset URL in the current environment, and an optional `mime_type` matching the file. Omit for text to image. |

    19→| `aspect_ratio` | Optional; defaults to `auto`, chosen from the content and references. Also accepts `X:Y`, with X and Y integers from 1 to 300 and a ratio from 1:3 to 3:1, inclusive. |

    21→| `n` | Optional integer from 1 to 10 per request; defaults to 1. Each image is a separate file. A grid or sheet of panels is one image. |
    22→| `output_format` | Optional; defaults to `jpeg`. Keep the default or explicitly set `jpeg`. Set `png` only when the user explicitly requests PNG. `jpg` and `jpeg` are equivalent, and the response reports `jpeg`. |
    23→| `output_file` | Optional base filename. Choose an unused name; the service supplies the extension and appends `-1`, `-2`, etc. for multiple images. |

    28→user asks for another tier, and request only the number of images the user wants.

# mcode-tools Master

App = Connector: both names refer to the same connected integration. An App in the product UI is a
Connector in the CLI; use `mcode-tools connector` to discover and call its tools.

Use the `mcode-tools connector` subcommands through the `bash` tool. The launcher is already on the
current runtime process PATH when this skill is available.

For every multimodal generation or understanding request, search Connector tools before saying the
capability is unavailable. Useful discovery keywords include `image`, `photo`, `video`, `audio`,
`music`, `document`, `generate`, `understand`, and `analyze`.

Use this skill for every App/Connector request, including an ordinary single call. The absence of

  request to use it.

  specialized external or connected-account data, look for a suitable App when no relevant dedicated
  tool is already known. App tools invoked through Bash count as dedicated tools. Ordinary knowledge
  questions, local-file tasks, and explicitly requested web searches do not require this discovery.

  Plugin. Neither a missing Plugin declaration nor an empty direct tool list proves an App is absent.

When you have a Matrix Drive `node_id` and need a fresh download URL, use the top-level command:


Upload a local file and get a temporary URL with the top-level command:
